name: Amazon Athena
oneLiner: Serverless SQL directly over files in S3 — no cluster to manage.
whatItIs: Athena runs SQL straight against files sitting in S3 — no servers, no loading, no cluster to size. You define a table over your Parquet/CSV/JSON in the Glue Data Catalog, then query it and pay only for the bytes scanned. It's built on Presto/Trino, so it's a distributed query engine, but you never see the machines. Athena is the go-to for ad-hoc exploration of lake data and for querying logs, without standing up a warehouse. Where Redshift is a warehouse you load into, Athena leaves the data where it is.

inPractice.narrative: Logs and events already sit as partitioned Parquet in S3. A crawler (or a table definition) registers them in the Glue Data Catalog, and analysts open Athena to run SQL — no infrastructure spun up, billed per query by data scanned. Results feed QuickSight dashboards or a notebook. It's the fastest way to ask a question of lake data without committing to a warehouse.

coreConcepts.detail: Athena reads files in S3 directly; there is no ingestion step and no copy of the data. The Glue Data Catalog holds the table schemas it queries against.
You pay per TB the query reads from S3. Columnar formats (Parquet/ORC), compression and partition pruning are not just performance — they directly cut the bill.
Hive-style partitions (e.g. dt=2026-07-01) let Athena skip irrelevant files. Partition projection computes partitions from a pattern so you don't have to register millions of them.
ANSI SQL with rich functions, joins across large datasets, and federated connectors to other sources. Athena engine v3 is current.
Isolate teams, set per-query data-scan limits and cost controls, and route results to specific S3 locations — the main guardrail against runaway spend.
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT and UNLOAD write query results back to S3 as Parquet, handy for building curated tables or exporting.

whenToUse: Ad-hoc SQL exploration of data already in S3, with no infrastructure to run.
Querying logs, exports and event data where a full warehouse is overkill.
Spiky or occasional analytics where paying per query beats a running cluster.
Building curated Parquet tables from raw data via CTAS.
Quick joins across lake datasets registered in the Glue Catalog.
whenNotToUse: Low-latency dashboards with many concurrent users hitting the same tables — a warehouse serves that faster.
Sub-second interactive queries — Athena has per-query startup and is scan-bound.
Heavy repeated queries over huge unoptimised data — the per-scan bill balloons; load into Redshift instead.
Row-level updates/transactions — it's read-oriented (Iceberg tables add some DML, but it's not an OLTP store).

keyFacts.label: Model
keyFacts.value: Serverless, distributed SQL (Presto/Trino) over S3 files.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per TB of data scanned (plus S3 request costs).

keyFacts.label: Catalog
keyFacts.value: Uses the Glue Data Catalog for table/schema metadata.

keyFacts.label: Formats
keyFacts.value: Parquet, ORC, CSV, JSON, Avro; Iceberg tables supported.

keyFacts.label: Ops
keyFacts.value: Nothing to provision, patch or scale.

pricingShape: Almost entirely per-TB-scanned: a query that reads 1 TB of CSV costs far more than the same query over well-compressed, partitioned Parquet reading 10 GB. There's no cluster to pay for when idle — zero queries means (nearly) zero cost, aside from stored data in S3. The whole cost game is data layout: columnar format, compression, partitioning and only selecting needed columns. Workgroup scan limits stop a careless SELECT * over the whole lake from becoming a surprise invoice.
gotchas: SELECT * over unpartitioned CSV scans everything and bills for it — the classic Athena cost trap.
Millions of tiny files kill performance and cost; compact into larger Parquet files.
Schema lives in the Glue Catalog — stale/incorrect partitions mean queries silently miss data (run MSCK REPAIR or use projection).
It's not built for high concurrency of low-latency queries; dashboards with many users may need a warehouse or caching.
Per-query startup latency makes it a poor fit for sub-second interactive apps.
